subject: CSF & Fluids
title: CSF Analysis: Pattern Recognition in Meningitis and Neurology
preview: Interpret CSF cells, glucose, protein and opening pressure together, not as isolated diagnostic cutoffs.

sections.title: Start with the patient
points: Evaluate contraindications and procedural safety before lumbar puncture; never delay urgent care for a critically unwell patient.
Compare CSF glucose with a near-contemporaneous blood glucose rather than treating the absolute number alone as definitive.

sections.title: Recognize common patterns
points: Bacterial, viral, tuberculous and fungal infections have overlapping but useful patterns in cell differential, protein and glucose.
Albuminocytological dissociation is associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome but may be absent early.

sections.title: Examination pitfalls
points: Normal or nearly normal early CSF cannot fully exclude dangerous infection.
Microbiologic methods and overall clinical suspicion may matter more than a memorized fixed cell-count cutoff.

quickRevision: Bacterial meningitis often causes neutrophil-predominant inflammation and lower CSF glucose, although early patterns can vary.
Viral meningitis more often has a lymphocyte-predominant pattern with relatively preserved glucose.
CSF results depend on sampling time, prior treatment, blood contamination, immune status and age.

quiz.question: Which CSF result can support bacterial meningitis in context?
options: No inflammatory cells in every case
Neutrophilic pleocytosis with low CSF glucose
A completely normal CSF profile in all cases
quiz.explanation: Bacterial meningitis commonly gives neutrophil-predominant CSF inflammation and a reduced CSF-to-blood glucose relationship, with exceptions after partial treatment or in early disease.
